title: This New Deal Masterpiece Must Be Saved
author: Robin Stephens
content:
![This New Deal Masterpiece Must Be
Saved](https://storage.ghost.io/c/65/af/65afbdb5-30bf-4286-acc4-9535069adb42/content/images/2026/08/wpa-
mural-cohen-building-washington-dc-1--1-.jpg)

When I showed up at the Wilbur J. Cohen Building in Washington DC to see the
murals by Ben Shahn and Seymour Fogel, I was told the building wasn't open to
the public. It was September 2025 and I was commencing my research on New Deal
art with a visit to these murals as well as the Archives of American Art held
by the Smithsonian Institute. I could probably have tried harder to get
security to let me see the murals, but my limited charm didn't work.

The Cohen Building was closed because it is awaiting sale or demolition.
Originally constructed between 1939 and 1940 to house the Social Security
Board, the building became the headquarters for various wartime agencies and
later served as the longstanding base of Voice of America. The building is in
need of substantial repairs and renovation work, estimated to cost half a
billion dollars, according to the General Services Administration. Not long
after Donald Trump began his second term, his administration put the building
on the chopping block.

Since my failed attempt at a visit, the media, campaigners, and politicians on
the hill have all called attention to the threat posed to the building and the
important works of New Deal art it houses. On July 14, 2026, Reps. Dina Titus
and Lloyd Doggett introduced a bill called Protecting Resources and Ensuring
Stewardship of Enduring Records of Visual Expression, or the PRESERVE Act.
Doggett cited the Cohen Building's "precious artworks that provide a visual
history of the struggle, opposition, and ultimately of progress across
generations of Americans." The bill would force the GSA, when attempting to
dispose of federal property, to identify artworks in the targeted building and
organize efforts to preserve them which may include removal and transfer to
museums or other facilities. But it would be difficult if not impossible to
relocate the Shahn and Fogel murals, which were done in fresco, painted onto
and into the wall itself.
